title: Why the centre drives the pieces back
comments: Since the pawn has not been moved to the centre, we may still regard the advance as pawn-less in our sense.
And now the faultiness of White's development may be seen, the Black pawns have a demobilizing effect.
bad at the outset, a piece moved twice
White is uncomfortably placed, at any rate from the point of view of the player with little fighting experience.
studyNotes: White brings a knight towards the centre. Both central pawns are still on their starting squares.
Black develops a knight too. So far, neither side has moved a central pawn.
The pawn opens a path for the bishop, but e3 is outside the four central squares: d4, e4, d5 and e5. This is what the author means by ‘pawn-less’ here.
Black occupies e5 with a pawn. Notice the contrast with White’s pawn on e3.
White develops the other knight to c3. Remember this square: Black’s d-pawn will attack it later.
Black develops the second knight while keeping the pawn on e5 in the centre.
White develops the bishop to c4. The question mark in the book warns that Black can gain time by attacking it with a pawn.
The pawn on d5 attacks the bishop on c4. White must spend time responding to that threat. The orange arrow shows the attack.
The bishop retreats from c4 to b3. White has now used two turns on this bishop, while Black has built a pawn centre.
The same pawn advances to d4 and now attacks the knight on c3. This is the ‘demobilizing’ effect: the centre drives developed pieces away. Step back twice to compare the two pawn attacks.
note: Opening chapter, §2, paragraph beginning ‘1. Kt-KB3, Kt-QB3’. The ten moves are transcribed from that paragraph and replayed from the normal starting position. Book excerpts are verbatim except surrounding punctuation; the separate learning notes and orange threat arrows are editorial explanations.
